clue.text: Poor Walter does talk big!.

indicators.note: poor here means in bad shape, so the surname is knocked into a new order

parts.note: Walter Pater, the Victorian essayist and critic, supplies his surname

explanation.surface: A man named Walter is mocked for boasting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' scrambles PATER, the surname of the essayist Walter Pater, which the clue calls up by his first name only.
explanation.definitionFit: To prate is to chatter boastfully and at length, which is what talking big amounts to.

clue.text: Gamy jams?

parts.note: estates kept for game birds and fruit spreads in jars share one name

explanation.walkthrough: Land reserved for game birds is a game reserve under another name, and jams are fruit kept in jars under the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: Jams are fruit conserves, and grounds kept for game birds share the same word.

clue.text: Hope to catch an early immigrant

definitions.meaning: to fish with rod and line, hoping for a bite
one of the Germanic people who settled in Britain in the fifth century

explanation.definitionFit: To fish is to try to hook something, and the Angles were Germanic settlers of early Britain.

clue.text: PM all-star occasions ?

parts.note: PM is the afternoon and night, and the occasions when the stars all come out are the times after sunset

explanation.surface: A prime minister's star-studded events.
explanation.walkthrough: PM looks like the Prime Minister but is post meridiem, after noon; all the stars appear at night.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the late parts of days, when the sky fills with stars.

clue.text: His teeth overcome

parts.note: in an old two-man sawpit one sawyer stood above the log, so the teeth of his saw cut from on top; overcome read as come over

explanation.surface: Someone is conquered by a man's teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: In a sawpit the senior man stood on top and guided the saw, so his saw teeth came from over the log; the phrase also means a person of distinction.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper man in a sawpit worked from above, so his saw teeth came down over the timber; the term also means a leading figure.

clue.text: Patmore's poem to young son initially

indicators.note: initially takes the opening letters of the two words that follow to

explanation.surface: A Victorian poet's verse written for his little boy.
explanation.walkthrough: Coventry Patmore's poem 'The Toys' is about punishing his young son. TO is given as it stands; 'initially' takes Y and S from 'young son'.
explanation.definitionFit: Coventry Patmore's best-known short poem is titled after a child's playthings.

clue.text: Expert Professor of History?

parts.note: a skilled adept, read playfully as a master of things gone by

explanation.surface: A specialist who teaches history at a university.
explanation.walkthrough: Read in two parts, it is a teacher of the past; as one term, a complete expert.
explanation.definitionFit: A past master is an adept, someone thoroughly skilled; split, it suggests a teacher of bygone times.

clue.text: Tree deity awaiting Cinderella

parts.note: the ash is a tree
Pan is the Greek god of the wild

explanation.surface: A woodland god waiting for the fairy-tale heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Cinderella' as 'cinder-ella': this tray under a grate waits to catch cinders.
explanation.definitionFit: The tray under a grate catches the cinders falling from the fire, a pun on the fairy-tale heroine.

clue.text: Rock-and-roll can provide many chats for him

indicators.note: rocking and rolling tosses the letters about until a new word is provided

explanation.surface: Rock music gives a man plenty to talk about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock-and-roll can provide' rearranges MANY CHATS; a boat rocks and rolls, so the indicator also fits the sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: The man is the one who rocks and rolls on a yacht, a sailor of pleasure boats.

clue.text: Brought down, not up

parts.note: demolished, sounding like its opposite, lifted, so not lifted

explanation.surface: Something lowered rather than raised.
explanation.walkthrough: This old spelling of razed, demolished, sounds like 'raised', which is what it is not.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an old spelling of razed, demolished, and sounds like its opposite, lifted.

clue.text: Cortez's peak hour television

parts.note: Keats's sonnet has stout Cortez stare at the Pacific with sharp sight, silent upon a peak in Darien; that gaze is his view from the summit

explanation.surface: A Spanish explorer's prime-time viewing schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats wrote of 'stout Cortez when with eagle eyes / He star'd at the Pacific … Silent, upon a peak in Darien'. 'Television' is taken literally as far-seeing.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats gives the conquistador keen hawk-like vision as he gazes out from a mountain summit, his own long-distance viewing.

clue.text: Kicking horses ?

definitions.meaning: in rugby and football, kicking an opponent's shins is hacking
riding horses for hire or ordinary use are called by this name

explanation.definitionFit: Hacking is kicking at a player's legs, and the same word names ordinary riding horses.

clue.text: Lady counsellor, one' eager for reform

indicators.note: for reform asks for the letters to be reshaped into something new

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A female adviser keen to change things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For reform' rearranges I (one) and EAGER. Egeria was the nymph who advised Numa, the legendary king of Rome, and her name came to mean any woman adviser.
explanation.definitionFit: Egeria, the nymph who guided King Numa of Rome, gave her name to any female adviser.

clue.text: As a neat head of hair might have disclosed

definitions.text: As a neat head of hair might have disclosed

parts.words: As a neat head of hair might have disclosed
parts.note: a tidy head of hair could announce '...', and the same sounds, run together, mean revealed or passed on

explanation.surface: What a well-groomed hairstyle might have revealed.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as I'M PARTED, the boast of tidily combed hair; joined up, it means told or made known, which fits 'disclosed'.
explanation.definitionFit: To impart news is to tell or reveal it, so the past tense means disclosed.

clue.text: Puzzling quarrelsomeness

parts.note: angry remarks traded in a row, or the grid puzzles themselves

explanation.walkthrough: Split, it is angry words exchanged in an argument; as one word, these very puzzles.
explanation.definitionFit: The grid puzzles share their name with angry words traded in a row.

clue.text: Plant productive of grape, highly-coloured, sour

parts.note: the grape grows on a vine
garish means gaudy and brightly coloured

explanation.surface: A description of a vine bearing gaudy, tart grapes.
explanation.definitionFit: Something with a taste like spoiled wine, acidic and tart, is sour.

clue.text: Henry-who built our canals ?

parts.note: Prince Henry of Portugal had this epithet, and the labourers who dug British canals bore the same title

explanation.surface: A man called Henry is asked whether he dug Britain's waterways.
explanation.walkthrough: Prince Henry of Portugal had this nickname; British canals were called navigations and their diggers took the name, shortened to navvies.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Henry of Portugal was so called, and canal diggers took the same name, later shortened to navvy.

clue.text: Southern gull or merganser

parts.note: mew is an old name for a gull

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher's note asking which seabird was spotted down south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gull' tempts as the definition, but it is MEW; the definition is the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: The smew is a small diving duck of the merganser group.

clue.text: Viburnum the tree by their roadside

definitions.text: Viburnum the tree by their roadside

parts.words: Viburnum the tree by their roadside
parts.note: the wayfaring tree is a hedgerow viburnum, named for the travellers who pass it on the road

explanation.surface: A botanical note on a viburnum growing by the road.
explanation.walkthrough: Viburnum lantana is called the wayfaring tree because it grows by roads that travellers walk.
explanation.definitionFit: Travellers on foot pass the hedgerow viburnum named after them.

clue.text: One is used in cutting hedge, too long

indicators.note: in cutting asks for a run of letters cut out from within the next words

explanation.surface: Someone trims an overgrown hedge with a blade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In cutting' takes the run EDGETOOL from inside 'hedge, too long'; the whole clue also describes the device.
explanation.definitionFit: Any bladed implement such as a chisel or axe is used for cutting.

clue.text: Break the vase but not the piggy-bank

indicators.note: break means smash to pieces, so the letters of the word vase are broken up

parts.note: the anagram fodder; that the answer also runs backwards through 'the vase' is a coincidence, not a hidden reversal

explanation.surface: Advice to smash a vase rather than your money box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break' rearranges VASE; the rest reads 'but [break] not the piggy-bank', and not breaking into your savings is what saving means.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping the money box intact means putting money by rather than spending it.

clue.text: Dominance of flexible canes in dancing mood

indicators.note: flexible means bendable, so the letters of canes bend into a new order

parts.note: dancy is an informal adjective for being inclined to dance

explanation.surface: Bendy canes swaying in a lively mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flexible' rearranges CANES to ASCEN; DANCY is a rare word for in the mood to dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascendancy is a position of controlling power over others.

clue.text: Heavenly praise for her

definitions.meaning: the hymn of glory to God in the highest, sung in the Mass

explanation.definitionFit: Gloria in excelsis is the hymn of glory to God, and it is also a woman's name.

clue.text: Manic-depressive boots

definitions.meaning: a bipolar life swings between elated peaks and dark troughs
these were laced ankle-boots of the nineteenth century

explanation.definitionFit: Manic depression is a life of peaks and troughs, and the same word once named laced ankle-length footwear.

clue.text: Tautological ram in an agitated state

parts.note: a tup is already male, so adding the male pronoun he says the same thing twice
tup is a dialect word for a ram

explanation.surface: A sheep given a needlessly repetitive description.
explanation.walkthrough: A tup is a male sheep, so calling it a he-tup is tautology.
explanation.definitionFit: Being worked up means flustered and anxious.

clue.text: French gratitude to a kingdom of old England

parts.note: merci is French for thank you

explanation.surface: A Frenchman thanks an ancient English realm.
explanation.definitionFit: Mercia was one of the Anglo-Saxon realms of the English Midlands.

clue.text: Surplice often soiled with pottery.

parts.note: a short surplice, and with terra, Latin for soil, in front it becomes baked-clay pottery

explanation.surface: A choirboy's vestment gets dirty from clay.
explanation.walkthrough: A cotta is a short surplice; put terra (earth, 'soil') before it and you have terracotta pottery.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a short church vestment, and with terra before it, baked clay ware.

clue.text: Divine finials despite our DIY efforts

definitions.text: Divine finials despite our DIY efforts

parts.words: Divine finials despite our DIY efforts
parts.note: Hamlet's line that a divinity shapes our final outcomes, rough-hew them how we will

explanation.surface: Ornamental tops made by God, despite our home improvements.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet says 'There's a divinity that shapes our ends, / Rough-hew them how we will': our rough-hewing is the DIY.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet's line says God shapes our final outcomes, whatever rough work we do on them.

clue.text: Galleryite surfacing from the underground ?

parts.note: a visitor to London's Tate gallery emerging from the Tube, or a spud dug up from the soil

explanation.surface: A gallery-goer climbing out of the Underground station.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is a London art gallery, so its visitor is punningly a Tate-r; a tater is also slang for a potato, which comes out of the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A tater is slang for a potato, a tuber lifted from the soil, and also jokingly a Tate gallery visitor.

clue.text: Nor recent maybe that casual meeting

indicators.note: maybe suggests the words given are only one possible arrangement of the letters

explanation.surface: A chance encounter that was neither long ago nor lately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' rearranges NOR RECENT; the result is a French word borrowed into English.
explanation.definitionFit: A rencontre is a chance encounter, from the French for meeting.

clue.text: Nine up on this for a classic race

definitions.text: Nine up on this for a classic race

parts.words: Nine up on this for a classic race
parts.note: the nine Muses dwelt on this Greek mountain, home of the arts of the ancient classical people

explanation.surface: Nine jockeys mounted on a horse for a famous Classic.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests horse racing (the Classics are Britain's big flat races); really the Nine are the Muses, up on their mountain, for the classical Greek people.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek mountain was the seat of the nine Muses, patrons of the arts of classical Greece.

clue.text: Onerous, though their tone is attractive

definitions.text: Onerous, though their tone is attractive

parts.words: Onerous, though their tone is attractive
parts.note: heavy burdens are onerous, yet add the word tone and you get the magnetic rock, which attracts iron

explanation.surface: Something burdensome yet pleasant-sounding.
explanation.walkthrough: Burdens are onerous; followed by STONE, the word gives loadstone, the magnetic iron ore, so 'their tone' is attractive in the magnetic sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavy burdens are onerous, and joined to stone they make the naturally magnetic ore.
